Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd.

First suppose that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\), so \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Then \(a^m\not\equiv1\pmod p\), while \((a^m)^2\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(p\) is odd, this implies \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Hence
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
If \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(a\) has order \(2m\), we have \(2m\mid2n\), and therefore \(m\mid n\). Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Put \(x=-a\), so \(x\) has the odd order \(m\) and \(a=-x\). Certainly
\[
a^{2m}=(-x)^{2m}=x^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Now suppose that \(a^n=(-x)^n\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(n\) were odd, then \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod p\). Squaring would give \(x^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid2n\). Because \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\), which would imply \(x^n\equiv1\pmod p\), a contradiction since \(p\) is odd. Therefore \(n\) is even. Then \(x^n=a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid n\). Since \(m\) is odd and \(n\) is even, \(2m\mid n\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\), and hence \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).

feedback.reason: The proof is correct. It uses that m=(p-1)/2 is odd, proves in the forward direction that (-a)^m≡1 and every exponent annihilating -a is divisible by m, and in the converse proves that every exponent annihilating a is divisible by 2m while a^(2m)≡1. Thus the claimed orders follow exactly.

problem.proof_text:
\begin{proof}

    Let $a$ a primitive root modulo $p$.

As $a^{p-1} \equiv 1(\bmod p), p \mid\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}-1\right)\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}+1\right)$, so $p \mid a^{(p-1) / 2}-1$ or $p \mid$ $a^{(p-1) / 2}+1$. As $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p, a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so

$$

a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1 \quad(\bmod p) .

$$

Hence $(-a)^{(p-1) / 2}=(-1)^{2 t+1} a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv(-1) \times(-1)=1(\bmod p)$.

Suppose that $(-a)^n \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, with $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Then $a^{2 n}=(-a)^{2 n} \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so $p-1\left|2 n, \frac{p-1}{2}\right| n$.

So $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$ modulo $p$.

Conversely, suppose that $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2=2 t+1$ modulo $p$. Let $2, p_1, \ldots p_k$ the prime factors of $p-1$, where $p_i$ are odd.

$a^{(p-1) / 2}=a^{2 t+1}=-(-a)^{2 t+1}=-(-a)^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1$, so $a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod 2)$.

As $p-1$ is even, $(p-1) / p_i$ is even, so $a^{(p-1) / p_i}=(-a)^{(p-1) / p_i} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)($ since $-a$ has order $p-1)$.

So the order of $a$ is $p-1$ (see Ex. 4.8) : $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$.

\end{proof}
problem.theorem: Consider a prime $p$ of the form $4 t+3$. Show that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ iff $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$.

conditions: N is a subgroup of G
rule_candidates.name: Quotient group criterion
rule_candidates.statement: If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.

rule_candidates.statement: If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.
